title: Falls of the Ohio
summary: At the Falls of the Ohio, Jeffersonville Limestone laid down by a Devonian sea about 390 million years ago made the only major rapids on the river.
bodyMarkdown:
The Falls of the Ohio were never a single waterfall. They were a run of rapids where the river dropped about 26 feet over two miles near present-day Louisville. An account of the [Falls of the Ohio National Wildlife Conservation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falls_of_the_Ohio_National_Wildlife_Conservation_Area) calls them the only barrier to navigation on the river in earlier times. That one obstacle shaped the geology lesson, the Native crossing and the city that grew beside it.

## A Devonian sea floor

The rapids cross shelves of hard Jeffersonville Limestone. The rock dates to about 387 to 380 million years ago, at the boundary of the Early and Middle Devonian. Then the region lay under a shallow inland sea about ten degrees north of the equator. Large tabulate and rugose corals lie exposed in lifelike positions, along with brachiopods, bryozoans and snails.

The beds are [one of the world's largest exposed Devonian fossil deposits](https://grokipedia.com/page/Falls_of_the_Ohio_National_Wildlife_Conservation_Area), and one account rounds their age to about 390 million years.

## A crossing place

Because the river was shallow here, the Falls made a natural ford. Bison herds [crossed](https://grokipedia.com/page/Falls_of_the_Ohio_National_Wildlife_Conservation_Area) on their way to salt licks, and people followed. Archaeological finds there include atlatls, adzes, pottery, fishing weirs and mussel middens. Native nations including the Shawnee and Miami used the Falls as a crossing point and a place to gather resources in the centuries before European contact.

## The choke point

For river traffic in the late 1700s and early 1800s, the rapids were a hazard. Boats relied on local pilots who knew the channels. The Falls are credited with the existence of Louisville and of Jeffersonville, Clarksville and New Albany on the Indiana side.

In 1778 [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/) set up camp on Corn Island near the Falls. About [175 Virginia militiamen left](https://grokipedia.com/page/George_Rogers_Clark) from there in June 1778 for the Illinois campaign. The settlers moved from the island to the mainland in 1779 and [named their town for King Louis XVI of France](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville,_Kentucky). In 1803 Meriwether Lewis met William Clark at the Falls to recruit men for the Corps of Discovery.

Engineering eventually tamed the rapids. The [Louisville and Portland Canal](/stories/louisville-and-portland-canal/), finished in 1830, carried boats around them. Later, the McAlpine Locks and Dam covered most of the falls.

## Kentucky today

The Falls were named a National Natural Landmark in 1966. In 1981 Congress made the area a National Wildlife Conservation Area, managed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. It is the only such area under the Corps. The Indiana side became the [Falls of the Ohio State Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/Falls_of_the_Ohio_State_Park) in 1990, with an interpretive center on geology, Native American history and the Lewis and Clark story.

The fossil beds are best seen at low water from August to October, and removing fossils is prohibited. Across the river, Louisville's waterfront still faces the old rapids.
